prompt: In the run, where did `daprd` sit relative to the shop's program?
hint: Think about what `--network container:shop` did.

choices.text: Inside the shop's Python process, loaded as a library
choices.why: There is no import of Dapr anywhere in `app.py`; the sidecar is a program of its own, in a container of its own.

choices.text: In a container of its own, sharing the shop's network namespace and its localhost
choices.why: Yes. That is why the metadata says it reaches the app at `127.0.0.1:8080`.

choices.text: In a container on `shop-net`, reached by the name `shop-dapr`
choices.why: It has no network of its own to be reached on; `docker port shop-dapr` printed nothing.

choices.text: As a service in Azure that the shop calls over the internet
choices.why: Nothing in the lab reached Azure; the sidecar ran on the laptop, beside the shop.

prompt: Port 3500 had to be published with `-p 3500:3500` when the shop's container started, before the sidecar existed. Why there?
hint: Look at what `docker port` printed for each container.

choices.text: Because Dapr refuses to start when its container has a published port
choices.why: Dapr has no opinion about Docker's ports; a container sharing another's namespace simply has none to publish.

choices.text: Because 3500 is the shop's own port and the sidecar listens elsewhere
choices.why: The sidecar listens on 3500; the shop listens on 8080.

choices.text: Because the sidecar joined the shop's namespace and has no network of its own to publish on
choices.why: Yes. Ports belong to a network namespace, and this one is the shop's.

choices.text: Because publishing it on the sidecar would clash with port 8080
choices.why: Two different ports cannot clash; the reason is that the sidecar has no namespace of its own.

prompt: Which of these were requests from the sidecar to the app, rather than from the app or the laptop to the sidecar? Choose all that apply.
hint: The shop's own log shows what reached it.

choices.text: `GET /dapr/config` on the shop
choices.why: Yes; the shop logged it with a 404.

choices.text: `GET /dapr/subscribe` on the shop, once a broker was loaded
choices.why: Yes; with a pub/sub component loaded the sidecar asks the app what it subscribes to.

choices.text: `GET /v1.0/healthz`
choices.why: That was `curl` on the laptop asking the sidecar about itself.

choices.text: `POST /v1.0/state/statestore`
choices.why: That goes the other way: a caller asking the sidecar to save state.

choices.text: `POST /orders` on a subscriber, carrying a CloudEvent
choices.why: Yes; delivery is the sidecar calling its app on the route the app named.

prompt: A container app runs in multiple-revision mode, with a new revision taking 10% of the traffic. Somebody changes `dapr.appPort`. What does Microsoft's documentation say happens?
hint: Dapr's settings are application-scope.

choices.text: A new revision is made with the new port, and takes no traffic until it is given some
choices.why: That is what a change to the template does. A Dapr setting is not part of a revision.

choices.text: No revision is made, and every existing revision is restarted with the new port
choices.why: Yes. So a Dapr change cannot be tried on 10% of the traffic first.

choices.text: Only the revision taking 10% restarts, as the latest one
choices.why: The documentation says all existing revisions are restarted.

choices.text: The change is refused until the app is back in single-revision mode
choices.why: Nothing in the documentation refuses it; it applies to every revision at once.

prompt: Container Apps starts the sidecar beside every replica, and your code reaches its HTTP API on `localhost`, on port ___.
hint: The same port you published on the shop's container.

prompt: The shop saved `order-1`. Billing's sidecar, loaded with the same `statestore` component, asked for `order-1` and got 204 with an empty body. Why?
hint: Look at the key Redis actually held.

choices.text: The state store is scoped to the shop, so billing reads an empty copy
choices.why: Nothing was scoped; billing loaded the component and reached the same Redis.

choices.text: Billing's sidecar looked for `billing||order-1`, and every key carries its app id in front
choices.why: Yes. The default prefix is the app id, so two apps on one store see only their own keys.

choices.text: Redis had not yet copied the value to billing's side
choices.why: There is one Redis and no copying; the key simply has a different name.

choices.text: The ETag on `order-1` belonged to the shop
choices.why: An ETag guards writes, and this was a read of a key that does not exist for billing.

prompt: Put the steps of the ETag run in the order they happened.
hint: The value ended at quantity 3.
items: a write carrying ETag 1 is accepted with 204
a second write carrying ETag 1 is refused with 409
trap: The refusal comes after the version moved: it is the stale 1 meeting a 2 that makes it a conflict.

prompt: On the Redis component, billing runs two replicas and audit runs one, all subscribed to `orders`. The shop publishes 5 orders. How many deliveries are made in total, counting every program that receives one?
hint: One consumer group per app id; replicas of one app share their group.

prompt: A bug makes `subscriber.py` answer 404 on `/orders`. What does Dapr's documentation say the sidecar does with a message delivered there?
hint: The answers it understands are SUCCESS, RETRY and DROP, and a status code says something too.

choices.text: Retries it until the app answers SUCCESS
choices.why: Retrying is what `RETRY` asks for; a 404 is read as a route that does not exist.

choices.text: Delivers it to the other subscriber instead
choices.why: Each app has its own copy; billing's failure does not move its message to audit.

choices.text: Drops it, and writes an error in the sidecar's log
choices.why: Yes. A wrong route loses messages, and the app's own log says nothing about it.

choices.text: Stops the subscription for that topic
choices.why: The subscription stays; each message that meets the 404 is dropped.

prompt: Match each piece with what it decides.
hint: One answer on the right belongs to none of them.

pairs.right: the name the code puts in the URL
which product the sidecar connects to
the settings that type needs, such as an address
what the sidecar subscribes to on the app's behalf

right_distractors: where the values themselves are kept

prompt: The first publish through the Service Bus component answered 500. What was it trying to do?
hint: Read the address in the error: the scheme and the port.

choices.text: Reach `localhost`, because the connection string named it
choices.why: The string named `servicebus`, and the error shows that host being reached.

choices.text: Send over AMQP to a queue `orders` that had not been declared
choices.why: `Config.json` declared it, and the request never got as far as AMQP.

choices.text: Check over HTTPS that the queue exists, so it could create it if not
choices.why: Yes. Entity management is on by default, and the emulator does not serve that endpoint.

choices.text: Deliver to `subscriber.py`, which had not been changed for Service Bus
choices.why: The failure was the publisher's, before any delivery; the subscriber needed no change at all.

prompt: After the swap to `pubsub.azure.servicebus.queues`, each of orders 2 to 6 reached billing or audit, never both. Why?
hint: What did the component map the topic `orders` to?

choices.text: Billing and audit ended up with the same consumer ID
choices.why: Their consumer IDs are their app ids, which differ, and they still shared the messages.

choices.text: The topic became one queue, both apps received from it, and a queue gives each message to one receiver
choices.why: Yes. The API stayed the same and the delivery became the queue's.

choices.text: The emulator balances load between receivers, as Azure would not
choices.why: A Service Bus queue in Azure hands each message to one receiver too.

choices.text: `disableEntityManagement` removed one of the two subscriptions
choices.why: It stops the component creating entities; there were never subscriptions, only the queue.

prompt: Which of these were the same before and after the swap to Service Bus? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare the two component files, and what the subscribers printed.

choices.text: `subscriber.py`
choices.why: Yes; not a line of it changed.

choices.text: The request that publishes, `/v1.0/publish/pubsub/orders`
choices.why: Yes; the same URL and body.

choices.text: The component's `type`
choices.why: It went from `pubsub.redis` to `pubsub.azure.servicebus.queues`.

choices.text: A copy of each order for each of the two apps
choices.why: On Service Bus queues the two apps shared one copy between them.

choices.text: The component's name, `pubsub`
choices.why: Yes; the code calls it by that name, so it had to stay.

prompt: The Service Bus component creates the queues and subscriptions it needs unless a metadata entry tells it not to: ___ set to `"true"`.
hint: It is the line appended with `printf`.

prompt: On Service Bus, with entity management off, the shop wants billing and audit each to receive every order, as they did on Redis. What does that take?
hint: Which Service Bus entity gives every interested reader its own copy?

choices.text: The queues component, with a different `consumerID` set for each app
choices.why: Their app ids already differed, which is what a consumer ID defaults to, and they still competed for the queue.

choices.text: Two component files called `pubsub`, one per app, each naming the same queue
choices.why: Both would read the one queue `orders`, and a queue still gives each message to one receiver.

choices.text: A higher `maxDeliveryCount` on the queue
choices.why: That is how often a failing message is retried, not how many receivers get it.

choices.text: The topics component, and a topic `orders` with subscriptions `billing` and `audit` declared beforehand
choices.why: Yes. Each app reads its own subscription, and with entity management off they must exist first.

prompt: In `dapr.bicep`, `componentType` is written `'pubsub.azure.servicebus.queue'`, singular. What happens, going by the run?
hint: The compiler checked one typo and not the other.

choices.text: The compiler warns with BCP089 and offers the plural
choices.why: BCP089 came for `appID`, a property the compiler knows. `componentType` is a plain string.

choices.text: It compiles in silence, and `daprd` refuses the type when it starts
choices.why: Yes. The open-source sidecar exited with `couldn't find message bus`; the template had been written without a word.

choices.text: It compiles, and the sidecar loads it as the queues component
choices.why: The sidecar in the run did not guess; it stopped.

choices.text: The compiler refuses to write `queue.json`
choices.why: `ls queue.*` listed `queue.json`; the template was written.

prompt: Billing subscribes through Dapr in Container Apps, with `minReplicas: 0` and no scale rule but the default one for HTTP. Nobody calls billing over HTTP. What happens to the orders the shop publishes?
hint: Who receives a message for an app that has no replica?

choices.text: Azure keeps billing's sidecar running on its own, to receive them
choices.why: The sidecar lives in a replica; with no replica there is no sidecar.

choices.text: The shop's sidecar delivers them to billing directly when it wakes
choices.why: Pub/sub goes through the broker; the publisher's sidecar never delivers to a subscriber.

choices.text: Container Apps refuses to deploy a Dapr subscriber that can scale to zero
choices.why: Nothing refuses it; it deploys, and receives nothing.

choices.text: They wait in the broker with no sidecar to receive them, until a replica starts
choices.why: Yes. That is why billing keeps one replica, or gets a scale rule on the queue's length.

prompt: What does the `scopes` list of a Dapr component in a Container Apps environment hold?
hint: The documentation is particular about which name it is.

choices.text: The names of the container apps allowed to load it
choices.why: Close, and wrong: the documentation says scopes are Dapr app ids, not container app names.

choices.text: The Dapr app ids that load it
choices.why: Yes; `shop` and `billing` in `dapr.bicep` are the `appId` values.

choices.text: The managed identities that may sign in through it
choices.why: The identity is named in `azureClientId`; scopes say which apps load the component.

choices.text: The revisions of an app that may use it
choices.why: Dapr settings belong to the app, not to a revision, and so does loading a component.

prompt: Match each cost of Dapr with where the lesson showed it.
hint: One piece of evidence on the right shows none of them.

pairs.left: a second process in every replica
a hop on every call through it
pairs.right: the median of `/healthz` higher through the sidecar
the entity-management error, in the sidecar and not the shop

right_distractors: a new revision for every change to a Dapr setting

prompt: In which of these does Dapr pay for itself?
hint: Look for the case where the same code really meets more than one backend.

choices.text: A Python service on one Service Bus namespace for good, needing sessions
choices.why: It gains a process and a hop and reaches sessions only through component metadata; the broker's own library serves it better.

choices.text: A nightly report run as a Container Apps job
choices.why: Dapr is not supported for Container Apps jobs at all.

choices.text: A service that must run exactly Dapr 1.17.16 in production
choices.why: Container Apps picks and upgrades the version; a pinned version is not on offer there.

choices.text: Teams in Python and Go, on Redis on laptops and Service Bus in Azure
choices.why: Yes: one file per environment, and one API for both languages.

prompt: Put the journey of one order from the shop to billing, on the Redis component, in order.
hint: It starts on the shop's localhost and ends on billing's.
items: the shop's sidecar wraps the order in a CloudEvent and adds it to the stream `orders`
billing's sidecar reads it through the consumer group `billing`
billing's sidecar posts it to `/orders` on billing's `localhost:8080`
trap: The envelope is added by the publisher's sidecar, before Redis; the subscriber receives it already wrapped.

prompt: An environment has three Dapr-enabled container apps, running 2, 2 and 4 replicas. How many `daprd` sidecars are running?
hint: One sidecar per replica.

prompt: Whatever the broker, a subscriber finds the order under `data`, because Dapr wraps every published message in an envelope of the open format called ___.
hint: Its `type` in the run was `com.dapr.event.sent`.

prompt: In Azure, the environment's `statestore` component has `scopes: ['shop', 'billing']`. A third app, audit, calls `/v1.0/state/statestore` and its sidecar answers that no state store is configured. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Which apps load a scoped component?

choices.text: Audit's managed identity has no role on the store
choices.why: A missing role fails when the store is used; a component that was never loaded is a different answer.

choices.text: Audit's app id is not in `scopes`, so its sidecar never loaded the component
choices.why: Yes. Scopes name the app ids that load a component, and audit is not one of them.

choices.text: Audit asks for keys prefixed `audit||`, which do not exist yet
choices.why: That gives 204 and an empty body, as billing got in the lab, not a missing store.

choices.text: The component was added without restarting audit's revision
choices.why: Even after a restart, a sidecar loads only the components scoped to its app id.
